UNICEF UK Baby Friendly Initiative, A guide to infant formula for parents who are bottle feeding: goodnight milks contain follow-on milk and cereal, 'are not necessary for any baby and there is no independent evidence to support the claim that they help babies settle'. fixes.old: • In 2024, the UK charity First Steps Nutrition Trust found these milks were the top source of free sugars for 12 to 18-month-olds who drink them, at 49.8% of their free sugar intake.
fixes.new: • In 2024, the UK charity First Steps Nutrition Trust found that formula milks, including growing-up and toddler milks, were the top source of free sugars for 12 to 18-month-olds who drink them, at 49.8% of their free sugar intake.
fixes.why: Sustain's report of the First Steps Nutrition Trust findings (20 September 2024) attributes the 49.8% figure to 'Formula including growing up and toddler milks', not to growing-up milks alone.

fixes.old: Toddler milk: half the free sugar for the toddlers who drink it
fixes.new: Toddler milk: more sugar and cost, with no extra benefit
fixes.why: Overclaim. The 49.8% figure covers all formula milks combined, and only 12 to 18-month-olds who drink them, so 'half the free sugar' for toddlers in general is not supported (First Steps Nutrition Trust via Sustain, 20 September 2024).

fixes.old: • After 12 months, toddler milk is not needed. Most contain more sugar and cost more than cows' milk.
fixes.new: • After 12 months, toddler milk is not needed. Most are high in free sugars and cost more than cows' milk.
fixes.why: The evidence is about free sugars (14 of 16 products exceed the free sugar limit at 350 ml) and cost, not total sugar compared with cows' milk, which contains natural lactose (First Steps Nutrition Trust via Sustain).

fixes.old: HMOs or GOS (added sugars and fibres modelled on breast milk)
fixes.new: HMOs or GOS (prebiotic carbohydrates meant to mimic those in breast milk)
fixes.why: 'Added sugars' is misleading in an article that warns about sugar. HMOs (human-identical milk oligosaccharides) and GOS (galacto-oligosaccharides) are prebiotic oligosaccharides, not added sugars in the nutritional sense (BfR Opinion 37/2022).

fixes.old: • Pour the water into the bottle first, then add powder with the scoop from that tin, levelled off, exactly as the label says.
fixes.new: • Pour the water into the bottle first, while it is still hot, then add powder with the scoop from that tin, levelled off, exactly as the label says.
fixes.why: Safety. NHS How to make up baby formula: 'Always put the water in the bottle first, while it is still hot, before adding the powdered formula.' The heat is what kills bacteria in the powder, so this should not be lost after the hand washing step.

'Just 3 firms account for over 90% of supply' is in the CMA interim press release of 8 November 2024, which is in the list.

Food Foundation 18 June 2025: £6.99 for 800 g at Aldi (Mamia) and Lidl (Lupilu), dearest £14.00 (Aptamil 1 at Co-op). The Food Foundation itself says 'twice as much'. 'More than twice' is true by 1p, so left unchanged.

First Steps Nutrition Trust figures (14 of 16 products over the free sugar limit at 350 ml, about £14 a month more than cows' milk) confirmed via Sustain. The First Steps page itself does not repeat the numbers.

Regulation 2016/127: applied from 22 February 2020, DHA mandatory, nutrition and health claims banned on infant formula (Article 8), infant and follow-on labels must be clearly distinct (Article 6(6)), still directly applicable in Northern Ireland, retained in GB. All confirmed by GOV.UK guidance updated 3 April 2024. For formulas made from protein hydrolysates the regulation only applied from 22 February 2022, a detail the article can omit.

Preparation steps match NHS (at least 1 litre fresh tap water, never reboiled, cool no more than 30 minutes so at least 70°C, water first, levelled scoop from the pack, cool under cold running water with the lid on, wrist test 'warm or cool, but not hot', discard leftovers, 1 feed at a time, no microwave, no sugar or cereals, bottled water not usually recommended, prep machines must deliver at least 70°C) and WHO (no less than 70°C, discard feeds not consumed within 2 hours).

Editor may wish to add 1 line: the NHS notes that some anti-reflux formulas are made up at lower temperatures on the manufacturer's instructions, so parents using a prescribed or specialist formula should follow the pack or their health professional. The keybox line 'Make feeds with water at 70°C or above' could otherwise appear to conflict.

NHS quote 'All infant formulas will meet your baby's nutritional needs, regardless of brand or price' is on the NHS Best Start in Life bottle feeding page (updated 23 December 2025), not the Types of formula page. Both are listed, so no change needed.
